newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB cuts wheat yield 0.5 bu/ac on Prairie drought.
newsitem.headline: CWB cuts wheat yield 0.5 bu/ac on Prairie drought.

text.p: Wheat yield prospects were reduced by 0.5 bushel per acre on Wednesday due to drought conditions on Canadian southeastern Prairie crops, Canadian Wheat Board weather and crop surveillance director Paul Bullock told Reuters.
"That area is dry enough that we think, even though the rest of western Canada is doing well, we're taking yields down half a bushel," Bullock said in an interview.
Prairie wheat fields typically yield about 30 to 32 bushels an acre but the CWB's estimate Wednesday projected yields of 29.5 to 31.5 bushels per acre.

Southeast Saskatchewan and southwestern Manitoba farmland usually produces more wheat than the Prairie average at between 32 to 35 bushels/acre because droughts occur less frequently there than in southern Alberta and the soil is richer than south Alberta's brown soil, Bullock said.
"In our opinion, those areas are now just starting to lose yield potential based on what's happened to date," he said. "If there's rain next week, it'll limit the losses."
"If there's no rain to the end of the month, it'll be significant and if there's no rain through July, it'll be quite a concern," Bullock added.

All wheat seeded area on the Prairies was seen 9.2 percent down at 28.22 million acres in 1997 from 31.08 million acres the year before, Statistics Canada said April 30. All wheat last year yielded 32.6 bushels per acre, StatsCan said.
Canola area was forecast to rise 32 percent to 11.858 million acres from 8.8 million, StatsCan said. Canola yield averaged 21.7 bu/ac last year, it said.
United Grain Growers Ltd was scheduled to issue its second seeding estimate at 1400 CDT/1900 GMT on Wednesday.
Saskatchewan and Manitoba were forecast to remain dry through Sunday, Environment Canada said.
A high pressure air mass blocking the passage of storm systems over the southeast Prairies was likened to a jet stream anomaly known as an Omega block, or dome of death.
"This is acting like an Omega block, it's just in a different part of the continent," Bullock said.
